title: The Bell of the Bell House
premise: Edmund Villalobos, a hospice nurse who has spent his career rationalizing the strange things the dying say, takes a temporary post at Bell House, a crumbling estate where the last resident, Agnes Marsh, is dying and refusing to sign her house over to the village trust. When the church bell that was melted down in 1911 begins ringing at night, Edmund learns it tolls for anyone who hears their name in it—and that Agnes's family invited something into Bell House generations ago to keep them powerful, a bargain renewed with every deathbed signature. As the villagers close ranks around their secret and the entity feeds on loyalty, Edmund must choose between protecting the found family he's accidentally built among the staff and exposing the truth. He holds out until sunrise by refusing to let Agnes sign alone, taking the bell's toll upon himself; the house falls silent, Agnes dies free, and Edmund—no longer invisible—stays on as the one who answers when it rings.
about_author: Elodie Okonkwo is a former palliative care volunteer from coastal Maine whose years sitting with the dying taught her that the last words are rarely the truest ones. She writes horror about institutions, inheritance, and the quiet violence of belonging.

chapters.title: The Counting
chapters.summary: Edmund arrives at Bell House on a rain-slicked evening, meeting head nurse Ruth Okafor and the dying Agnes Marsh, who counts backwards under her breath without ever reaching zero. Edmund's POV establishes his professional detachment and his rule: never believe the patients. Emotional beat: wary competence masking loneliness.

chapters.title: Paperwork
chapters.summary: Solicitor Mr. Fenwick arrives pressing Agnes to sign the house over to the village trust before she dies; she refuses with surprising ferocity. Edmund notices the staff exchange glances whenever the papers appear. His POV. Emotional beat: first sense that the house runs on secrets older than its residents.

chapters.title: A Ring With No Rope
chapters.summary: At 3 a.m. Edmund wakes to the church bell ringing though the tower stands empty—the bell was melted down in 1911, as a plaque cheerfully confirms. Only he and young caretaker Tomas seem to hear it. Edmund's POV. Emotional beat: the crack in his unbelief, papered over with exhaustion.

chapters.title: The Staff of Bell House
chapters.summary: Edmund shares tea with cook Marisol, gardener Ivo, and Tomas, learning they're all misfits hired cheap and kept close—a family of strays, as Ruth says. They warn him gently not to go out when the bell rings. Alternating Edmund and Tomas POV. Emotional beat: warmth he didn't ask for, starting to take root.

chapters.title: What Agnes Remembers
chapters.summary: Agnes, lucid for an hour, tells Edmund about her grandmother's funeral in 1911, when the bell 'gave itself up' so the family could keep the house through hard winters. She calls it a debt, not a gift. Edmund's POV. Emotional beat: dread dressed as history.

chapters.title: The Village That Watches
chapters.summary: Edmund walks into town for supplies; shopkeepers are warm but evasive, and the vicar, Reverend Hale, questions him too closely about Agnes's condition and the signing. Edmund realizes the whole village is waiting for her death. His POV. Emotional beat: the vertigo of being seen and assessed.

chapters.title: Names in the Bronze
chapters.summary: Tomas shows Edmund the melted bell's surviving fragment, kept in the chapel crypt, etched with names—including, freshly cut, Edmund's own. The bell rings while they stand there. Tomas's POV reveals he's heard it since childhood. Emotional beat: terror shared becomes intimacy.

chapters.title: Loyalty of the Strays
chapters.summary: Ruth confronts Edmund: the staff know what the bell is and stay anyway, because Bell House took them in when nowhere else would. She asks him to stop digging or leave. Edmund's POV. Emotional beat: the theme sharpened—loyalty purchased with silence.

chapters.title: Fenwick's Bargain
chapters.summary: Fenwick corners Edmund, revealing the trust isn't about land but continuity: whoever holds the house renews the invitation, and the village prospers only while the signatures keep coming. He offers Edmund money to ensure Agnes signs. Edmund's POV. Emotional beat: temptation framed as kindness.

chapters.title: The First Toll Taken
chapters.summary: Groundskeeper Ivo goes out during the ringing to fix a broken gate and doesn't come back; they find him at dawn, aged decades, mouth full of grave-dirt, alive but hollowed. The staff grieve him like family. Edmund's POV. Emotional beat: grief weaponized into fear of defiance.

chapters.title: Agnes Refuses Again
chapters.summary: Agnes, weaker, tells Edmund why she won't sign: her mother signed and lost her sister to the bell, and Agnes means to be the last Marsh, ending the debt even if it ends the village's luck. Edmund's POV. Emotional beat: admiration curdling into alarm at the cost.

chapters.title: The Vicar's Sermon
chapters.summary: Hale preaches publicly on gratitude and obligation, staring at Edmund; afterward villagers shun the Bell House staff in the street. Ruth admits the entity isn't evil exactly—it keeps its bargains, which is worse. Tomas's POV. Emotional beat: the found family tightening into a besieged garrison.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: In the crypt records Edmund finds the original 1911 petition: the village, starving, asked the Marshes to invite 'a keeper' across, and the bell was its anchor and its voice. It counts backwards because it is always counting down to collection. Edmund's POV. Emotional beat: the truth arriving like cold water.

chapters.title: Ruth's Confession
chapters.summary: Ruth admits she once tried to flee with her daughter; the bell rang her name for three nights until she returned, and her daughter doesn't speak to her now. She begs Edmund not to make the same choice alone. Her POV. Emotional beat: loyalty revealed as trauma bond, love still real inside it.

chapters.title: The Signing Scheduled
chapters.summary: Fenwick returns with witnesses and a date: Agnes will sign the morning after next, and the village will attend. Agnes asks Edmund, quietly, to sit with her that night and not let her hand be guided. Edmund's POV. Emotional beat: a dying woman's trust placed in a man who believes nothing.

chapters.title: The Long Night Begins
chapters.summary: The staff gather in Agnes's room against protocol—Marisol brings food, Tomas brings the crypt fragment, Ruth brings her old rosary. At midnight the bell begins and does not stop. Multiple POVs braided. Emotional beat: siege intimacy, candlelight against bronze.

chapters.title: The Bell Calls Each Name
chapters.summary: Through the night the bell names them one by one: Marisol nearly walks out, Tomas bleeds from the ears, Ruth recites her daughter's name like armor. Edmund realizes it can't find purchase on him because he believes nothing—but that's fraying. Rotating POVs. Emotional beat: each character's loyalty tested at its weakest seam.

chapters.title: Fenwick at the Door
chapters.summary: Near dawn Fenwick and Hale arrive with papers and lanterns, insisting the signing happen now, in the dark, 'for everyone's good.' The staff form a line at the bedroom door. Edmund's POV. Emotional beat: power's corruption made polite, and ordinary people refusing it.

chapters.title: Climax: The Zero Hour
chapters.summary: As Agnes's count reaches single digits, the bell speaks in her dead sister's voice, offering to spare the staff if she signs. Edmund, believing at last and choosing anyway, puts his own name forward in place of hers—taking the toll. The bell rings his name once, fully, and stops. Edmund's POV. Emotional beat: sacrifice as the only honest signature.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Dawn comes gray and quiet. Agnes dies minutes later, unburdened, her hand in Edmund's; the crypt fragment's names have all faded except his, now worn smooth like an old scar. Fenwick retreats; Hale looks smaller. Edmund's POV. Emotional beat: exhausted peace, grief and relief indistinguishable.

chapters.title: Aftermath: The Empty Tower
chapters.summary: The village prospers a little less; some resent Edmund, others bring bread. Ruth stays, Tomas laughs again, Marisol plants Ivo's garden back to life. The house belongs to no trust—it belongs to whoever tends it. Tomas's POV. Emotional beat: found family chosen freely, no longer bought.

chapters.title: The One Who Answers
chapters.summary: Months later, a new patient arrives at Bell House and murmurs about hearing bells. Edmund sits with her, listens, and this time does not look away. Far off, faintly, something remembers how to ring—and Edmund, keeper now, is ready to answer. His POV closes the book. Emotional beat: belief accepted as vocation, horror transmuted into care.
